 JUDGMENT
The complainant company has filed this private complaint under section 200 of Cr.P.C. against the accused company for the offence punishable under section 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act.

2. The brief facts of the complainant's case are as follows:
It is alleged that the complainant is a private limited company which manages R.L Fresh Chicken which is the unit of the Prakruthi Protein Foods India Pvt. Ltd.

sentences.text: The complainant alleged that the accused and the father-in-law of the accused who were managing the business activities independently requested the complainant to supply live boiler birds in the month of January-2021 to J.R. Boiles.
On the request of the accused the complainant agreed to supply the same as per the mutual understanding and conditions.
The complainant further alleged that the accused initially agreed to pay on daily basis and the accused was irregular in making payment.
The accused placed the order and issued cheque to clear the balance.
As on 04.04.2021 the total outstanding balance was Rs.11,50,000/- and out of the said amount the accused made part payment of Rs.1,00,000/- and agreed to clear the remaining balance within 15 days.

It is further alleged by the complainant company that, the accused issued the cheque bearing No.
123659 dated 06.07.2021 for Rs.10,50,000/- drawn on Canara Bank, Vivekananda Nagar Branch,
Bengaluru in favour of the complainant.

The complainant presented the said cheque on 06.07.2021 for encashment through drawee bank as per the request of the accused and the same is dishonoured and returned to the complainant by the endorsement, dated 07.07.2021 with a shara of " Funds Insufficient".
3.
Thereafter, the complainant issued legal notice, dated 26.07.2021 to the accused calling upon him to pay back Rs.10,50,000/- within 15 days from the date of receipt of the notice.
The said notice sent to the first address returned unserved with a reason of "Insufficient address returned to sender".
The notice sent to the second address was duly delivered on 28.07.2021.
Even after the issuance of notice, the accused neither replied nor made any payment.
By alleging that the accused intentionally not made any payment and the complainant having no other option has filed the present case by Prakruthi Protein Foods India Pvt Ltd vs Anand.

The plea of the accused recorded by this court.

The accused also filed application under Sec. 145 (2) of NI Act by praying for permission to cross-examine the PW.1 which came to be allowed and the PW.1 was cross- examined by the accused.

Thereafter, the accused was explained about all the incriminating circumstances available against him by framing the statement under section 313 of Cr.P.C.

6. Heard the arguments.

7. On the basis of above contentions and documents, the following points that arise for my consideration are:
1) Whether the complainant proves beyond all reasonable doubts that the accused has issued cheque bearing No. 123659 dated 06.07.2021 drawn on Canara Bank,

2) What order?
8. My findings to the above points are as under:
Point No. 1 : In The Negative Point No. 2 : As per the final order for the following reasons.

Point No. 1 :- It is much relevant to discuss about the ingredients of section 138 of N.I. Act to constitute the offence under this Act.
10. To substantiate his case, the manager of the complainant company examined as PW.2 and Ex.P1 to 10 are marked in favour of the complainant.
First, for the purpose of establishing the prima facie case, if we perused the documentary evidence filed by the complainant which were marked as Ex.P1 to 10, the Ex.P1 is a cheque, dated 06.07.2021.
The said Ex.P1 was presented and returned unpaid as per endorsement dated 07.07.2021, which is within the stipulated period.
As such, The requirement under section 138(a) of N.I. Act is fulfilled.
Further, upon presentation of the said cheque, the drawee bank has given endorsement that the said cheque was returned unpaid for the reason of "Funds Insufficient" as per Ex.P2.
Thereafter, the complainant has issued legal notice, which is marked as Ex.P3.
Ex.P3 is a written legal notice, dated 26.07.2021.
The cheque was dishonored and returned unpaid as per Ex.P2 dated 07.07.2021.
The legal notice was issued on 26.07.2021, which is within 30 days of the receipt of information of cheque being unpaid as per Ex.P2.
Further as per Ex.P.4 the Ex.P.3 legal notice was posted on 27.07.2021.
Hence, the requirement under section 138(b) of N.I. Act is fulfilled.
The notice was delivered on the second address of the accused on 28.07.2021.
Thereafter the complaint was filed on 09.09.2021.
Hence, The requirement under section 138(c) R/w. Sec. 142 (b) of N.I. Act is also fulfilled.

Accordingly, the prima facie procedure as envisaged under Sec. 138 & 142 of NI Act is complied by the complainant in respect of Ex.P1 cheque.
11.

In this case even though the issuance of legal notice and service of legal notice as claimed by the complainant is duly served, the accused has neither given any reply nor denied the address mentioned in the legal notice as incorrect.

In the absence of any reply notice and written objections,
the cross-examination of PW.1 and the evidence of accused are the main source to know the defence of the accused.

12. By considering the materials available on record the accused has taken two major defence i.e.,
firstly the accused denies the cheque and stated that Ex.P1 cheque does not belongs to him.

Secondly, there is no financial transaction with the complainant and has never issued any cheque to the complainant.
13.

Coming to the first defence of the accused, the accused has denied and stated that the Ex.P.1 cheque does not belongs to his account and he never had any bank account in Canara Bank,
Vivekananda Nagar branch.
The presumption under Sec.138 of NI Act raises only when the cheque and signature is admitted by the accused.

Keeping the said evidence of PW.1 in this regard, the accused examined the Manager of Canara Bank, Vivekanagar branch as DW.2 wherein he produced the Ex.D16 letter and Ex.D.17 Account statement of A/c No.1702101019653 of Canara Bank, Vivekananda Nagar Branch wherein he stated that the said account belongs to one Suman Kumar K.

15. The present case is filed by the complainant by alleging the commission of an offence punishable under Sec.138 of NI Act.

To know the ingredients of Sec.138 of NI Act the same is hereby reproduced for better appreciation of the point under consideration 138. Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency, etc., of funds in the account.--
Where any cheque drawn by a person on an account maintained by him with a banker for payment of any amount of money to another person from out of that account for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debtor other liability, is returned by the bank unpaid, either because of the amount of money standing to the credit of that account is insufficient to honour the cheque or that it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that account by an agreement made with that bank, such person shall be deemed to have committed an offence and shall, without prejudice to any other provision of this Act, be punished with imprisonment for 4[a term which may be extended to two years'], or with fine which may extend to twice the amount of the cheque, or with both:
Sec.138 of NI Act starts with a word where, and to consider the commission of an offence the cheque has to be drawn by a person on a account maintained by him.
These words presupposes the condition that to attract the offence under Sec.138 of NI Act drawing of a cheque by the person who has an account of the said cheque is the primary condition.
In this case the complainant stated that the accused issued Ex.P.1 cheque towards the amount due by him.
But has not lead any independent evidence to show that the Ex.P1 cheque belongs to the accused account.
It is the primary burden of the complainant to show that the Ex.P1 cheque belongs to the accused.
Once the said primary burden is discharged then the presumption follows the Ex.P.1 cheque.
In this case when the accused specifically denied the cheque the complainant has not adduced any evidence to show that the Ex.P.1 cheque belongs to Prakruthi Protein Foods India Pvt Ltd vs Anand.

17.

As already noted hereinbefore, in para 3 of the complaint, there is a clear averment that the cheque in question was issued from an account which was non-existent on the day it was issued or that the account from where the cheque was issued "pertained to someone else".
As per complainant's own pleadings, the bank account from where the cheque had been issued, was not held in the name of the appellant and
therefore, one of the requisite ingredients of Section 138 of the Act was not satisfied.
By applying the above precedent to the case on hand the complainant has not made any efforts to prove that the Ex.P.1 cheque belongs to the bank account of the complainant.
19. The cause of action to attract the penal provision of Sec.138 of NI Act will arise only when the cheque in question belongs to the accused.
The complainant is under the burden of proving its case beyond reasonable doubt.
The evidence of DW.2 created the cloud on the case of the complainant to consider that the said Ex.P1 cheque belongs to the accused.
The complainant has not taken any steps to clear the said cloud.
20. Coming to the point of alleged transactions and relationship between the complainant and accused, the accused denied the alleged transactions with the complainant and also issuance of cheque.
Until the complainant shows that Ex.P1 cheque belongs to the accused the other points will not arise for consideration.

For the sake of argument if the issuance of cheque is admitted by the accused and the said cheque is not belongs to the accused then also the penal provision of Sec.138 of NI Act does not attracts on the accused.
21. The accused has taken specific defence denying the cheque and signature on the Ex.P.1.
The said defence is also supported by the evidence of DW.2.

In spite of specific denial and the evidence of DW.2 in support of the same, the complainant not summoned and examined the Manager of Canara Bank, Vivekananda Nagar branch to show that the Ex.P1 cheque belongs to the accused.

In this regard if we rely on Section 114 of Evidence Act which states as follows;
Section 114.
Court may presume existence of certain facts.

The Court may presume the existence of any fact which it thinks likely to have happened, regard being had to the common course of natural events, human conduct and public and private business,
in their relation to the facts of the particular case.

8 Illustrations

The Court may presume - (g) that evidence which could be and is not produced would, if produced, be unfavourable to the person who withholds it;
When a party has evidence with them to prove the existence of few facts and if such party has not produced those documents and offers no explanation of non production of such evidence the adverse inference has to be drawn.

By applying the said principle of law in this case the complainant has not made any minimum effort to show that the Ex.P1 cheque belong to the accused which in turn shows that the evidence of DW.2 has to be accepted.
22. By considering this, no doubt that the complaint is filed by alleging the commission of offence punishable under Sec. 138 of NI Act.
No doubt that Sec. 138 of NI Act has the favorable presumption in favour of the complainant regarding the existence of legally recoverable debt.
But as discussed above, the accused can create the doubt over the case of the complainant by cross-examining the complainant or by producing probable defence.
The complainant is under the burden of proving beyond reasonable doubt whereas the accused is under the onus of proving his defence on the basis of preponderance of probabilities.

23. The learned counsel for complainant relied on the below judgments in support of their arguments by praying to draw the presumption in favour of the complainant and thereby convict the accused for the said offence.
A.I.R. 2010 SC 1898 Rangappa V/S Mohan.
(2018) 8 SCC 469 between T.P. Murugan (Dead)
through legal representatives V/s Bhojan.

In my humble opinion the above two quoted judgments are not applicable to the present case on hand as the complainant failed to prove the cheque belongs to the accused and thereby failed to establish the commission of offence.
Only after the proving of two facts i.e., cheque belongs to the accused and the signature only then the presumption can be drawn.
But the said two points are not established by the complainant.
24. Before proceeding further, in the trial of NI Act cases the more burden is casted on the accused to prove his defence.
The accused has to discharge his burden by raising the probable defence.
Mere stating of a fact is not sufficient to discharge his burden.
The accused can discharge his burden by adducing the defence evidence or by bringing out the latches in the case of the complainant itself by cross-examining the complainant.

The Hon'ble High Court of Karnataka in the case of Criminal Appeal No.2526/2009 - M/s. Shriram Transport Finance Co. Ltd. Vs. Sri H. Yallappa Naik, wherein Hon'ble High Court has held that:
"It is well settled principles of law that the accused need not prove his case beyond reasonable doubt as it is incumbent on the complainant to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt.

25. The ratio laid down in the above case is very much applicable to the case on hand.

The non- performance of some act by the accused cannot be in any manner taken as a lapse on the part of the accused and to hold that the inaction on the part of the accused itself is sufficient to convict the accused.
Because, it is the burden on the complainant to bring home the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt.

26. Further, in the case reported in (2014) 2 Supreme court cases 236- John K Abraham-V/s Simon C. Abraham and another,wherein the Hon'ble Supreme Court was held as hereunder:

1)that he had the requisite funds for advancingthe sum of money/loan in question to accused 2) that the issuance of cheque by accused in support of repayment of money advanced was true, and 3) that the accused was bound to make payment as had been agreed while issuing cheque in favour of complainant-In present case,complainant not aware of the date when substantial amount of Rs.150000/- was advanced by him to appellant- accused- Respondent complainant failed to produce relevant documents in support of the alleged source for advancing money to accused- complainant also not aware as to when and where the transaction took place for which the cheque in question was issued to him by accused-complainant also not sure as to who wrote the cheque and making contractor statement in this regard-In view of said serious defects/Lacunae in evidence of complainant,judgment of High court reversing acquittal of accused by trial court, held was perverse and could not be sustained-Acquittal restored."

28. In another decision reported in ILR 2009 KAR 1633 in between Kumar Exports V/s Sharma Carpets, wherein it was held that:
"Negotiable Instruments Act-1881- Sections 138and 139- Presumption under Section 118 and139- How to be rebutted- Standard of proof required for rebuttal-HELD, rebuttal does not require proof beyond reasonable doubt-something probable has to be brought on record-Burden of proof can be shifted back to the complainant by producing convincing circumstantial evidence- Thereafter the said presumption arising under Section 118 and 139 case to operate- To rebut said presumption accused can also rely upon presumption under Evidence Act, 1872 section 114 (common course of natural events, human conduct and public and private business)."

Crl.Apl. No.879/2023 between Ashok Shwakramani & others V/s State of Andhra Pradesh &
another "6.It is also necessary to note the averments made in Paragraph 8 of the complaint in which the second respondent stated that the statutory notice of demand was not served on the accused.

7.In fact, the service of notice of demand is a condition precedent for filing a complaint in view of clause (c) of Section 138 of the NI Act.

This is one ground on which the complaint must fail."
29.
It is clear that by these precedent as quoted above, the criminal jurisprudence does not expects the accused to rebut the presumption or to prove his defence beyond reasonable doubts.
By all these reported judgments, it is clear that if the accused make out any probable defence is sufficient to disprove the case of the complainant or to rebut the presumption.
The accused for discharging the burden of proof placed upon him need not to examine himself.
The accused may discharge his burden by bringing the negative facts in the case of the complainant by cross-examining him.
30. The evidence available on record shows that Ex.P.1 cheque does not belongs to the accused.
No evidence is placed by the complainant to impeach the credibility of the evidence adduced through DW.2.
By considering all these facts, the accused successfully probabalized his defence.
At the cost of repetition,by placing my reliance on the above quoted judgments, I would like to say once again that the accused need not to be proved his defence on beyond reasonable doubts.

ORDER

opennyai_summary.facts: The complainant company has filed this private complaint under section 200 of Cr.P.C. against the accused company for the offence punishable under section 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act.
opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
In this case even though the issuance of legal notice and service of legal notice as claimed by the complainant is duly served, the accused has neither given any reply nor denied the address mentioned in the legal notice as incorrect.
In the absence of any reply notice and written objections,
the cross-examination of PW.1 and the evidence of accused are the main source to know the defence of the accused.
12. By considering the materials available on record the accused has taken two major defence i.e.,
firstly the accused denies the cheque and stated that Ex.P1 cheque does not belongs to him.
Secondly, there is no financial transaction with the complainant and has never issued any cheque to the complainant.
13.
The presumption under Sec.138 of NI Act raises only when the cheque and signature is admitted by the accused.
In the present case as there is specific denial by the Prakruthi Protein Foods India Pvt Ltd vs Anand.
These words presupposes the condition that to attract the offence under Sec.138 of NI Act drawing of a cheque by the person who has an account of the said cheque is the primary condition.
But has not lead any independent evidence to show that the Ex.P1 cheque belongs to the accused account.
It is the primary burden of the complainant to show that the Ex.P1 cheque belongs to the accused.
Once the said primary burden is discharged then the presumption follows the Ex.P.1 cheque.
In this case when the accused specifically denied the cheque the complainant has not adduced any evidence to show that the Ex.P.1 cheque belongs to Prakruthi Protein Foods India Pvt Ltd vs Anand.
It is the primary burden of the complainant to prove that the Ex.P.1 cheque belongs to the accused.
In spite of specific denial by the accused,
the complainant has not taken any steps to prove that Ex.P.1 cheque belongs to the accused.
Nothing prevented the complainant to take summons to the Vivekananda Nagar branch Manager to substantiate and to discharge its burden to show that the Ex.P.1 cheque belongs to the accused.
9. It is manifest that to constitute an offence under Section 138 of the Act, the following ingredients are required to be fulfilled:
(i) a person must have drawn a cheque on an account maintained by him in a bank for payment of a certain amount of money to another person from out of that account:
(ii) The cheque should have been issued for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability;
(iii) that cheque has been presented to the bank within a period of six months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity whichever is earlier;
(iv) that cheque is returned by the bank unpaid, either because of the amount of money standing to the credit of the account is insufficient to honour the cheque or that it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that account by an agreement made with the bank;
(v) the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque makes a demand for the payment of the said amount of money by giving a notice in writing, to the drawer of the cheque, within 15 days of the receipt of information by him from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid;
(vi) the drawer of such cheque fails to make payment of the said amount of money to the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque within 15 days of the receipt of the said notice;
10. Being cumulative, it is only when all the afore-mentioned ingredients are satisfied that the person who had drawn the cheque can be deemed to have committed an offence under Section 138 of the Act.
Thus, there is hardly any dispute that the cheque, subject matter of the complaint under Section 138 of the Act, had not been drawn by the appellant on an account maintained by him in the Indian Bank, Sonepat branch.
The complainant is under the burden of proving its case beyond reasonable doubt.
Prakruthi Protein Foods India Pvt Ltd vs Anand.
The accused has to discharge his burden by raising the probable defence.
Mere stating of a fact is not sufficient to discharge his burden.
The accused can discharge his burden by adducing the defence evidence or by bringing out the latches in the case of the complainant itself by cross-examining the complainant.
The Hon'ble High Court of Karnataka in the case of Criminal Appeal No.2526/2009 - M/s. Shriram Transport Finance Co. Ltd. Vs. Sri H. Yallappa Naik, wherein Hon'ble High Court has held that:
"It is well settled principles of law that the accused need not prove his case beyond reasonable doubt as it is incumbent on the complainant to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt.
The non- performance of some act by the accused cannot be in any manner taken as a lapse on the part of the accused and to hold that the inaction on the part of the accused itself is sufficient to convict the accused.
Because, it is the burden on the complainant to bring home the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt.
Crl.Apl. No.879/2023 between Ashok Shwakramani & others V/s State of Andhra Pradesh &
another "6.It is also necessary to note the averments made in Paragraph 8 of the complaint in which the second respondent stated that the statutory notice of demand was not served on the accused.
opennyai_summary.decision:
For the foregoing reasons, I proceed to pass the following:
ORDER
In exercise of powers vested under Sec. 255 (1) of Cr.P.C. 1973 the accused is acquitted for the offence punishable under Sec.138 of Negotiable Instruments Act.
The accused is not found guilty of an offence punishable Under Sec. 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act and in the result, the complaint filed by the complainant under Sec.200 of Cr.P.C. is hereby dismissed.
The bail bond and surety bonds stands cancelled.
